newsitem.title: USA: Alternative fuel approved for urban bus systems.
newsitem.headline: Alternative fuel approved for urban bus systems.

text.p: A new brand of biodiesel fuel - certified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency - will not make buses run on time, but it will make them run cleaner.
The EPA has certified Envirodiesel, a blend of diesel and soybean oil, as the first alternative fuel for use in meeting the Clean Air Act requirements for urban buses.

"Under the rules," EPA spokeswoman Lucy Edmondson said, "urban transit systems must eliminate particulate matter. Using this system they can bring their buses into compliance." There is not a specific deadline for compliance, she said, "the EPA expects that as transit systems overhaul their buses, they will bring them into compliance."

Buses built after 1993 already comply with the EPA standards, but the majority of city-owned fleets consist of buses that were bought prior to 1993. It is those buses, the EPA believes, that can benefit from the retrofit and use of biodiesel fuel.
Envirodiesel's maker, Twin Rivers Technologies, a privately-held, Quincy, Mass.-based company, estimated there are 56,000 buses in U.S. city transit systems.

Its blend consists of 20 percent soybean oil and 80 percent diesel fuel, said the company's president Jim Ricci. He estimated that the market could reach 90 million gallons annually by the 2002, when the strictest regulations of the Clean Air Act come into effect.
A gallon of diesel fuel costs about $0.60, while Envirodiesel will cost about $1.25 a gallon.
Twin Rivers is already testing its product - a catalytic converter kit and fuel - in Miami, Boston and New York City.

"We're going to have to come into compliance," said Andrew Brennan, a spokesman for the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which in a preliminary study found that using Envirodiesel would save the Commonwealth $14 million over other options to refit or replace the system's 1,000 buses, most of which were bought before 1993.

Sandy Amores, who is in charge of operations for Florida's Metro Dade County 603 bus system, said in a telephone interview that a two-month test of the system, which was still underway, had revealed no major problems.

"We never told the drivers about the new fuel and we've had no feedback. No one has complained about low power or foul odor," Amores said. Some two-thirds of the Metro Dade County fleet was bought prior to 1993.

Charles Seaton, a spokesman for New York City's Transit Authority, which operates 3,700 buses that average two miles a gallon on diesel fuel, said the city is in talks with Twin Rivers and is also experimenting with using buses powered by compressed natural gas.
